teleprompter_script.act_1: Welcome to The Sound Above. I am Mike Hall. This is Episode 0: Mike Hall on our Northern Illinois Field Dispatch under the high-tension wires. In October 2026, I walked out underneath 345,000-volt transmission lines in Northern Illinois with a smartphone to record a field dispatch on software craftsmanship and identity. When I checked the footage back at my desk, the audio sounded completely destroyed: deafening 60 Hz electromagnetic hum, corona arcing, and an apparent three-and-a-half-minute clock drift. Trashing the footage and reshooting is the standard advice. But working through that recording became a living case study in what happens when we lean on modern AI models, and why the bottleneck in engineering is never generation: it is verification.
teleprompter_script.act_2: I started with a simple thirteen-word query in a browser, then brought it into Gemini Flash through the terminal. The model immediately leapt into action: generating cascaded Butterworth filter equations, calculating exact duration ratios, and asserting with supreme, effortless confidence that the audio clock had drifted by twenty percent. It gave me shell scripts, math, and complete DSP pipelines. And it was all totally wrong. In Hollywood, investigators yell 'Enhance!' and pixels appear out of thin air. In software, that wishful thinking produces hallucinated AI slop. It reminds me of the Dell Studio XPS laptop I carried during the 2009 Obtiva days, with the sticker that read: 'Typing is not the bottleneck.' In 2026, generating code is not the bottleneck either. The bottleneck is domain understanding.
teleprompter_script.act_3: The container reported 21 minutes of video and only 18 minutes of audio. The model assumed linear drift and handed me atempo=0.837. When I tested the audio in my headphones, it was slurred and completely out of sync. So we went back to ground truth: high-FPS frame extraction, Whisper subtitle alignment, and audio waveforms. What actually happened? At 18 minutes, I said 'Thank you' and wrapped the talk. The remaining three and a half minutes was just me walking with the camera running in silence. The speech was at 1.0x normal speed all along. When AI models project effortless competence, how do you verify where competence ends and plausible falsehood begins? You verify with empirical tests, not conversational trust.
teleprompter_script.act_4: Let us look at the raw recording from the phone (YouTube ID: 7YeFpKn5FbU). Notice the stereo separation. Modern smartphones have dual microphones for noise suppression. The secondary microphone at the top was an unshielded inductive loop antenna, picking up 65 times more electromagnetic rumble from the overhead transmission towers than the bottom microphone. The bottom left mic had clean speech buried under the noise. Once we split the stereo channels and discarded the antenna track, we had clean speech. We did not need exotic neural de-reverberation models. We needed basic hardware acoustics.
teleprompter_script.act_5: Here is the lesson for engineering in the AI era. We took the output of the model, threw away the hallucinations, and machined the working parts into a deterministic seven-stage filter in shell and Python. It runs in 40 milliseconds. It muxes the audio back into the master container with zero generational video re-encoding loss. We spent less than a dollar and twenty-five cents in subscription compute, instead of hiring an audio post-production house. Generative models are fantastic at rapid hypothesis synthesis, like a 3D printer in a machine shop. But you cannot leave your software inside a chat window. You have to machine it into deterministic, testable code you own and control.
teleprompter_script.act_6: That is the spirit of The Sound Above. Across this 37-episode series, we are going to rewatch fifteen years of conversations from the Software Craftsmanship movement, from the early Chicago user groups to the AI horizon, examining how developers tackled architecture, testing, and autonomy before commercial platforms took over. Full transcripts, telemetry, and companion code are open at just3ws.com. If you want to help support our independent hosting and archive preservation, check out patreon.com/whoistechcmty. In Episode 1, we dive into the very first room: Sergio Pereira and Chicago Alt.NET. Until next time: keep your feedback loops fast, and verify your code.

teleprompter_script.act_1: Welcome to The Sound Above. I am Mike Hall, and this is Episode 1 of our technical rewatch series. Today we are going back to November 19, 2011, on-site at Software Craftsmanship North America at the Swissotel in downtown Chicago. My very first guest when we launched the UGtastic interview series was Sergio Pereira, the organizer of Chicago Alt.NET. There is a reason I asked Sergio to sit down first. Chicago Alt.NET was the very first user group I ever walked into, and the first stage where I ever gave a technical talk.
teleprompter_script.act_2: To understand why that room mattered, you have to remember what enterprise .NET felt like in 2007 and 2008. Most corporate shops treated Microsoft's default box products as the law. If a tool or workflow did not ship inside Visual Studio or MSDN, you were told not to touch it. In April 2007, David Laribee published the Alt.NET Manifesto, and that October developers gathered in Austin for the first Alt.NET Open Spaces, which Martin Fowler wrote about in his Bliki. Sergio brought that exact spirit to Chicago. On the second Wednesday of every month at 6:30 PM, right when commuters could still catch the Metra train back to the suburbs, about 25 of us took the elevator up to Redpoint Technologies on the 84th floor of the Sears Tower. On November 12, 2008, I stood up in that room and gave my first talk on NHaml alongside Adam Tybor presenting on the Spark view engine.
teleprompter_script.act_3: Here is the question that guides our rewatch today: How do working engineers build practical autonomy inside corporate environments without waiting for vendor permission? Alt.NET was never about hating .NET. As Sergio says right at the start of this tape, we were developers who liked .NET, used it every day, and wanted to bring continuous improvement, automated testing, NHibernate, StructureMap, CodeSharp, and IronRuby into our daily work. When Richard Banks and the community organized the Entity Framework v1 Vote of No Confidence, and Jeremy Miller wrote his March 2008 MSDN Magazine piece on Alt.NET, they proved that practitioners could hold vendor tooling accountable to real engineering standards.
teleprompter_script.act_4: Let us roll the 2011 hallway conversation with Sergio Pereira (YouTube ID: qOHdZKz1WFw). Listen to how Sergio describes the charter of the group: not bringing in polished marketing speakers, but encouraging regular team developers to take the talks they gave at lunch with their coworkers and share them with a room of peers who wanted to see a better way to build software.
teleprompter_script.act_5: How does this connect to where we sit in 2026? In 2008, the default vendor trap was drag-and-drop designer wizards that hid coupling and made unit testing impossible. Today, the default vendor trap is black-box cloud AI generation that produces thousands of lines of unverified code while hiding the domain boundaries underneath. The lesson from Chicago Alt.NET is unchanged: tools are instruments, not religions. You do not accept a workflow just because a vendor ships it as the default. You keep your domain models clean, you run your own fast local verification loops, and you judge every tool by whether it holds up under test.
teleprompter_script.act_6: Thank you for joining Episode 1 of The Sound Above. You can read the full interactive transcript with Sergio Pereira, along with links to David Laribee's 2007 Manifesto, Martin Fowler's Austin notes, and Jeremy Miller's retrospectives, right on the Episode 1 page at just3ws.com. To help support our independent compute and archive preservation, visit patreon.com/whoistechcmty. In Episode 2, we sit down with Ray Hightower of ChicagoRuby to talk about grassroots hospitality and opening doors across communities. Until next time: keep your feedback loops fast, and your code humane.

teleprompter_script.act_1: Welcome back to The Sound Above. I am Mike Hall, and this is Episode 2. Today we return to SCNA 2011 at the Swissotel in Chicago for my conversation with Ray Hightower, the founder of WisdomGroup and organizer of ChicagoRuby and WindyCityRails. If Sergio Pereira gave me my first user group room in the Sears Tower, Ray Hightower was the ambassador who opened the door to the entire Chicago Ruby and software craftsmanship community.
teleprompter_script.act_2: In late 2008, I was working remotely as Principal Developer at Business Decisions, Inc., maintaining a multi-tenant HR platform and coordinating with developers in Uruguay. I reached out to Ray, and we met up halfway at Midway Restaurant. I was still a Microsoft .NET developer at the time. Ray did not gatekeep or lecture me about platforms. He just opened his MacBook right there at the diner table, fired up his terminal, and showed me Cucumber running plain-English acceptance tests. Before we left, he invited me to ChicagoRuby and told me about an open Friday pairing session happening up in Libertyville at a small consultancy called 8th Light.
teleprompter_script.act_3: Our core inquiry for Episode 2 is simple: What makes a technical community endure across decades, and why does hospitality matter so much when engineers are crossing paradigm boundaries? When you are spending forty hours a week in a legacy stack, walking into a room full of people using a different operating system, a different editor, and a different language is intimidating. Ray understood that hospitality is not a soft extra. It is the bridge that lets working engineers cross over and learn new disciplines without feeling like outsiders.
teleprompter_script.act_4: Let us roll the SCNA 2011 conversation with Ray Hightower (YouTube ID: XZqGbf5C76E). Pay attention to how intentionally Ray thinks about structure, venue logistics, and linking downtown city developers with suburban user groups across Chicagoland.
teleprompter_script.act_5: In 2026, when so much engineering work happens in isolated remote home offices behind AI chat prompts, the risk of professional isolation is higher than it was in 2008. Autonomous code generation can synthesize boilerplate in seconds, but it cannot sit across from you at a diner table, show you a better testing workflow, or introduce you to the peers who will change the trajectory of your career. We still need human ambassadors and open rooms where engineers share their actual workbenches.
